questions.q: A photograph of the Earth taken from space shows mostly blue, with patches of another colour. According to the chapter, which colour in such a picture stands for land?
questions.a: Brown

questions.q: Meena reads that water covers 'almost three-fourths' of the Earth's surface and land covers 'a little over one-fourth'. She says both figures cannot be right, because three-fourths and one-fourth already make the whole surface. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Both are right: water is a little less than three-fourths and land a little more than one-fourth, so together they still make one whole.
o: Both are right: water is a little less than three-fourths and land a little more than one-fourth, so together they still make one whole.
Meena is right: together the two figures come to more than the whole surface, so one of them must be wrong.
Both are right only because clouds cover the part of the surface that is neither land nor water.
Both are right only for the Northern Hemisphere; the Southern Hemisphere is covered fully by water.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When seen from outer space, the Earth appears mostly blue.
Reason (R): Almost three-fourths of the Earth's surface is covered with water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Oceans and continents are spread equally between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
II. The smaller extensions of the oceans have names such as 'sea', 'bay' and 'gulf'.
III. Both oceans and continents play a vital role in shaping the climate of the Earth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: Explain the term 'continent' as the chapter uses it, and give one example of a continent.
questions.a: A continent is a large continuous expanse of land. Example: Africa (or any one of Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America).
s: States that a continent is a large continuous expanse of land
Gives one correct continent, such as Africa or Asia

questions.q: True or False? 'The Northern Hemisphere has more land than the Southern Hemisphere.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Land and water are not spread equally between the two hemispheres; the Northern Hemisphere holds more of the land, so the Southern Hemisphere has more of the water.
s: Gives the verdict True
Explains that land and water are not distributed equally between the hemispheres and the Northern one holds more land

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) About how much of the Earth's surface is covered with water? (b) About how much of it is land? (c) Why did early astronauts call the Earth the 'blue planet'?
questions.a: (a) Almost three-fourths. (b) A little over one-fourth. (c) Because water covers most of the surface, the Earth looks mostly blue from outer space.
s: (a) Almost three-fourths of the surface is water
(b) A little over one-fourth is land
(c) The Earth looks mostly blue from space because water covers most of it

questions.q: The chapter says oceans and continents 'affect all aspects of life', including human life. Trace this idea as a chain of three links, using what the chapter says, from oceans and continents to human life.
questions.a: Link 1: oceans and continents play a vital role in shaping the climate of the Earth. Link 2: climate affects all plants and animals. Link 3: so human life is affected too, and we see this in our history, our culture and our daily lives.
s: Link 1: oceans and continents shape the Earth's climate
Link 2: this affects all plants and animals
Link 3: therefore human life too, seen in history, culture and daily life

questions.q: Sort each place into one of the chapter's terms: 'ocean', 'smaller extension of an ocean (sea, bay or gulf)' or 'continent'. Add a few words of reason for each. (a) the Pacific (b) the Arabian Sea (c) Africa (d) the Bay of Bengal (e) Australia
questions.a: (a) Pacific: ocean, the largest of the five oceans. (b) Arabian Sea: a smaller extension (a sea), part of the Indian Ocean west of India. (c) Africa: continent, a large continuous expanse of land in the seven-continent list. (d) Bay of Bengal: a smaller extension (a bay), part of the Indian Ocean east of India. (e) Australia: continent, one of the seven in the most widely used list.
s: (a) Pacific is an ocean
(b) Arabian Sea is a smaller extension of the Indian Ocean
(c) Africa is a continent
(d) Bay of Bengal is a smaller extension of the Indian Ocean
(e) Australia is a continent

questions.q: (a) Which hemisphere has more land, according to the chapter? (b) A sailing crew wants to spend as much of a long voyage as possible on open water, far from land. Using your answer to (a), in which hemisphere should they plan most of the voyage, and why?
questions.a: (a) The Northern Hemisphere. (b) The Southern Hemisphere: since the Northern Hemisphere holds more of the land, the Southern Hemisphere has less land and more water, so there is more open water to sail on.
s: (a) Names the Northern Hemisphere
(b) Chooses the Southern Hemisphere because it has less land and so more water

questions.q: Which ocean does the chapter name as the third largest of the five oceans?
questions.a: The Indian Ocean

questions.q: The crew of a ship in the middle of the Pacific Ocean run short of drinking water, though they are surrounded by water on every side. Why can they not simply drink the seawater?
questions.a: Seawater is salty and unfit for drinking by most land animals, including humans.
o: Seawater is salty and unfit for drinking by most land animals, including humans.
Seawater in the open ocean is mostly frozen into glaciers.
The oceans hold only a very small share of the planet's water.
Seawater is groundwater, so it lies too deep below the ship.

questions.q:
Match each place in Column A with where it lies, as given in the chapter, in Column B.
Column A: 1. Arabian Sea  2. Bay of Bengal  3. Asia  4. Africa
Column B: a. the part of the Indian Ocean to the east of India  b. the part of the Indian Ocean to the west of India  c. the limit of the Indian Ocean to the north  d. the limit of the Indian Ocean to the west

On a blank world map, a student finds an ocean whose limits are Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east. She labels it 'Pacific Ocean' because 'the biggest ocean must be the one beside India'. Which correction is right?
questions.a: It is the Indian Ocean, the third largest; those are the chapter's limits of the Indian Ocean.
o: It is the Indian Ocean, the third largest; those are the chapter's limits of the Indian Ocean.
It is the Atlantic Ocean, the second largest; it lies between Africa and Australia.
It is the Southern Ocean, the fourth largest; it lies to the south of Asia.
The label is right, because the largest ocean is the one closest to India.

questions.q: (a) Name the largest and the smallest of the five oceans. (b) What other name does the chapter give for the Southern Ocean?
questions.a: (a) The Pacific Ocean is the largest and the Arctic Ocean is the smallest. (b) The Antarctic Ocean.
s: (a) Names the Pacific as largest and the Arctic as smallest
(b) Gives 'Antarctic Ocean' as the other name

questions.q: (a) Name the two parts of the Indian Ocean that lie on either side of India. (b) A map-maker colours these two parts differently from the Indian Ocean and labels all three as separate oceans. Using (a), what is her mistake?
questions.a: (a) The Arabian Sea to the west and the Bay of Bengal to the east. (b) The Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal are parts of the Indian Ocean, not oceans of their own; the chapter names only five oceans, so the map should show them as part of the Indian Ocean.
s: (a) Names the Arabian Sea (west) and the Bay of Bengal (east)
(b) Explains that both are parts of the Indian Ocean, not separate oceans

questions.q: A school atlas draws thick black lines between the five oceans. A visitor from a fishing town says, 'These lines are not walls; the oceans are really one.' Give three pieces of evidence from the chapter that support the visitor.
questions.a: 1. The lines that divide the oceans on a map are no more than conventions; the natural world does not follow them. 2. Seawater constantly flows across different oceans. 3. Many plant and animal species are found across more than one ocean.
s: States that the dividing lines are only conventions that nature does not follow
States that seawater constantly flows across the oceans
States that many plant and animal species are found in more than one ocean

questions.q: Three clues describe one ocean. Clue 1: it is smaller than the Atlantic Ocean. Clue 2: it is larger than the Southern Ocean. Clue 3: Asia is its limit to the north and the Bay of Bengal is one of its parts. (a) Which oceans fit Clue 1? (b) Which of these also fit Clue 2? (c) Does Clue 3 agree with your answer to (b)? Name the ocean.
questions.a: (a) The Indian, Southern and Arctic Oceans are smaller than the Atlantic. (b) Of these, only the Indian Ocean is larger than the Southern Ocean (the Arctic is the smallest). (c) Yes: Asia is the northern limit of the Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal is part of it, so the ocean is the Indian Ocean.
s: (a) Lists the Indian, Southern and Arctic Oceans
(b) Narrows it to the Indian Ocean only
(c) Confirms with Clue 3 and names the Indian Ocean

questions.q:
A science park in Bhubaneswar builds a giant floor map of the world's oceans. It gives each ocean a number of floor tiles by its size rank: the largest ocean gets 50 tiles, the second 40, the third 30, the fourth 20 and the smallest 10. The Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal get 4 tiles each and are painted the same colour as the ocean they belong to. The areas are separated only by thin painted lines.
(a) How many tiles does the Pacific Ocean get?
(b) How many more tiles does the Atlantic Ocean get than the Arctic Ocean?
(c) In the colour of which ocean are the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal painted?
(d) A visitor asks why the map uses thin painted lines instead of walls between the oceans. Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 50 tiles, since the Pacific is the largest ocean. (b) The Atlantic is second (40 tiles) and the Arctic is smallest (10 tiles), so 40 - 10 = 30 more tiles. (c) The Indian Ocean's colour, since both are parts of the Indian Ocean. (d) The oceans are not really separate: the lines between them are only conventions, and seawater constantly flows across them, so thin lines show this better than walls.
s: (a) 50 tiles for the Pacific, the largest
(b) 40 - 10 = 30 more tiles
(c) The colour of the Indian Ocean
(d) Oceans are interconnected; boundaries are only conventions

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Indian Ocean is the third largest of the five oceans.
Reason (R): The Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal are parts of the Indian Ocean.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: What is a tsunami, as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: A huge and powerful wave, generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean
o: A huge and powerful wave, generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean
A violent storm with extreme rainfall or very strong winds that forms over the ocean
The seasonal rain that India expects every summer, which comes from the ocean
A large mass of white cloud that forms over the ocean and moves towards the land

questions.q: A student's project says: 'The tsunami of 26 December 2004 struck India and 13 other countries, began with an earthquake in India and took more than two lakh lives.' Which single correction makes it match the chapter?
questions.a: The earthquake that caused it was in Indonesia, not India.
o: The earthquake that caused it was in Indonesia, not India.
It struck only 13 countries in all, counting India.
It took more than two thousand lives, not two lakh.
It began with a cyclone, not with an earthquake.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tsunami can submerge coastal areas far away from the place where it started.
Reason (R): A tsunami is caused by very strong winds blowing over the ocean.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. India has its own National Disaster Management Authority to deal with all kinds of disasters.
II. The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System is run by India alone.
III. Tsunamis can often be detected before they hit a coast.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: Differentiate between a cyclone and a tsunami, giving one point about each from the chapter.
questions.a: A cyclone is a storm: a violent event with extreme rainfall or very strong winds that can damage coastal regions. A tsunami is a huge, powerful wave, generally caused by a strong earthquake or volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean.
s: Describes a cyclone as a violent storm with extreme rainfall or very strong winds
Describes a tsunami as a huge wave caused by an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption

questions.q: True or False? 'A disaster that strikes the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a matter for the islands alone, so India's National Disaster Management Authority would not deal with it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The National Disaster Management Authority is India's own body to deal with all kinds of disasters, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are part of India (they were among the places in India severely affected by the 2004 tsunami).
s: Gives the verdict False
Explains that the Authority deals with all kinds of disasters in India and the islands are part of India

questions.q: A newspaper in 2024 marks the anniversary of the tsunami of 26 December 2004. (a) How many years after the tsunami is 26 December 2024? (b) The chapter says 'more than two lakh people' lost their lives. Write two lakh in figures with Indian commas. (c) The tsunami struck India and another 13 countries. How many countries is that in all?
s: (a) 20 years
(c) 14 countries

questions.q: A coastal district in Tamil Nadu is preparing a wall chart titled 'How we face the ocean's disasters'. Using the chapter, write the four sections of the chart: (a) the two ocean disasters and what each is; (b) why tsunamis must be prepared for even though they are rare; (c) how an early warning system such as the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System helps; (d) the role of the National Disaster Management Authority.
questions.a: (a) Cyclones are storms with extreme rainfall or very strong winds; tsunamis are huge waves generally caused by strong undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. (b) Tsunamis are rare but very destructive: they can travel thousands of kilometres and submerge coastal areas, as in 2004 when Tamil Nadu's coast suffered much damage and loss of life. (c) Tsunamis can often be detected before they hit a coast; the warning system, to which many countries including India contribute, gives time to take measures to protect lives and property. (d) The Authority is India's own body for handling all kinds of disasters that lead to loss of life and property.
s: (a) Describes both a cyclone and a tsunami correctly
(b) Rare but very destructive, travel far and submerge coasts, with the 2004 example
(c) Early detection gives time to protect lives and property; many countries contribute
(d) The Authority handles all kinds of disasters in India

questions.q:
A farmer on the Odisha coast keeps a diary for one year. From June to September, 820 mm of monsoon rain falls and he gets a good paddy harvest. In October, a cyclone with very strong winds and extreme rain damages 30 of his 120 coconut trees and floods his fields for 6 days. His son, who works in a town 300 km inland, says the family should sell the coastal farm and buy land inland.
(a) According to the chapter, where do the monsoon rains that watered his paddy originate?
(b) What fraction of his coconut trees did the cyclone damage?
(c) How was the October event different from a tsunami?
(d) Should the family move inland? Give a decision with one point on each side, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) In the ocean. (b) 30 out of 120 = one-fourth of the trees. (c) A cyclone is a storm with very strong winds or extreme rain; a tsunami is a huge wave caused by a strong earthquake or volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean. (d) Either decision is accepted with both sides weighed, for example: moving inland would reduce damage from cyclones and tsunamis, which strike coastal regions; but the same ocean gave the monsoon rain behind his good harvest, the cyclone hurt only one-fourth of the trees, and warnings and disaster management can protect lives, so staying is reasonable.
s: (a) The monsoon rains originate in the ocean
(b) 30/120 = one-fourth
(c) Cyclone is a storm of wind and rain; tsunami is a wave from an undersea earthquake or eruption
(d) Makes a decision supported by one point on each side from the chapter

questions.q: Read this paragraph from a student's notebook: 'In 2004 a cyclone caused by an earthquake in Indonesia struck India and 13 other countries. Such disasters come with no warning at all, so nothing can be done before they strike. That is why India leaves disaster work to each coastal village. Luckily the ocean never brings India anything good either.' Evaluate the paragraph: (a) name the event correctly; (b) correct the claim about warnings; (c) correct the claim about who handles disasters in India; (d) correct the last sentence; (e) state which facts in the paragraph are right.
questions.a: (a) It was a tsunami, not a cyclone: a cyclone is a storm, while a tsunami is a huge wave caused by an undersea earthquake. (b) Tsunamis can often be detected before they hit a coast; early warning systems such as the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System help take measures to protect lives and property. (c) India has its own National Disaster Management Authority to deal with all kinds of disasters. (d) The ocean also brings the monsoon rains India expects every summer, without which agriculture and all life would suffer. (e) It is right that the 2004 disaster began with an earthquake in Indonesia and struck India and 13 other countries.
s: (a) Names the event as a tsunami and separates it from a cyclone
(b) Tsunamis can often be detected early; early warning systems help
(c) India has the National Disaster Management Authority
(d) The ocean brings the monsoon rains on which agriculture depends
(e) Keeps the Indonesia earthquake and the 14 countries as correct

questions.q: Which count of continents does the chapter say is the one most widely adopted and used?
questions.a: Seven continents

questions.q: A student writes the seven-continent list as: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, Eurasia. Which change makes her list correct?
questions.a: Replace Eurasia with South America.
o: Remove Antarctica, since it is not an inhabited continent.
Remove Europe, since it is part of Asia.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with what it stands for in the chapter's counts of continents in Column B.
Column A: 1. Eurasia  2. America  3. Africa-Eurasia  4. Antarctica
Column B: a. Europe and Asia taken as one continent  b. North America and South America taken as one continent  c. Africa, Europe and Asia taken as one continent  d. a continent that appears on its own in every one of the four counts
A student notices that 'Asia' is written by its own name in only one of the chapter's four counts of continents. Which count is it, and why do the others not show it?
questions.a: The seven-continent count; the other three join Asia with Europe as Eurasia, and the four-continent count joins Eurasia with Africa as well.
o: The seven-continent count; the other three join Asia with Europe as Eurasia, and the four-continent count joins Eurasia with Africa as well.
The six-continent count; the seven-continent count joins Asia with Europe as Eurasia.
The four-continent count; the other three join Asia with Africa.
The five-continent count; the six- and seven-continent counts call it America.

questions.q: Name the seven continents in the list that the chapter says is the most widely used.
questions.a: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.
s: Names any four of the seven correctly
Names all seven correctly with no extra or joined continent

questions.q: (a) What does the world map show about Europe and Asia as land? (b) Then why are they generally counted as two continents?
questions.a: (a) They form a single landmass. (b) For historical and cultural reasons: Europe's evolution has been very different from Asia's, so they can be seen as two continents (though geologists often regard them as one, Eurasia).
s: (a) States that Europe and Asia form a single landmass
(b) Gives the historical and cultural reason: Europe's evolution differs from Asia's

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Between which two numbers can the count of continents lie, according to the chapter? (b) What name do geologists often give to Europe and Asia taken together? (c) In the four- and five-continent counts, what are North America and South America together called?
questions.a: (a) Between four and seven. (b) Eurasia. (c) America.
s: (a) Four and seven
(b) Eurasia
(c) America

questions.q: A quiz asks: 'Name the chapter's count in which Africa is a continent on its own but North America is not.' Rahul answers 'the six-continent count'. Check his answer: (a) in which counts is Africa on its own? (b) in which counts is North America not on its own? (c) Is Rahul right? Give the correct count and what it joins.
questions.a: (a) Africa is on its own in the five-, six- and seven-continent counts (the four-continent count joins it into Africa-Eurasia). (b) North America is not on its own in the four- and five-continent counts, which use 'America'. (c) No. Only the five-continent count meets both conditions; it joins North and South America as America and Europe and Asia as Eurasia. The six-continent count keeps North America separate.
s: (a) Five, six and seven
(b) Four and five
(c) Rahul is wrong; the answer is the five-continent count, joining the Americas and Eurasia

questions.q: Four cards in a quiz box each show one list of continents. For each card, say which of the chapter's counts (four, five, six or seven) it shows. (a) Africa, America, Antarctica, Australia, Eurasia (b) Africa-Eurasia, America, Antarctica, Australia (c) Africa, Antarctica, Australia, Eurasia, North America, South America (d) Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America
questions.a: (a) The five-continent count. (b) The four-continent count. (c) The six-continent count. (d) The seven-continent count.
s: (a) Five-continent count
(b) Four-continent count
(c) Six-continent count
(d) Seven-continent count

questions.q: Three students count the continents on the same world map. Ravi gets 7, Salma gets 5 and Tenzin gets 4. Each of them used one of the counts given in the chapter. (a) What did Ravi join, if anything? (b) Which landmasses did Salma join? (c) What did Tenzin join beyond what Salma joined? (d) Explain how all three can be right about the same map. (e) Which count should a class atlas use, and why?
questions.a: (a) Nothing: Ravi kept Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America separate. (b) Salma joined North and South America as America, and Europe and Asia as Eurasia. (c) Tenzin also joined Africa with Eurasia, giving Africa-Eurasia. (d) The land is the same; continents can be counted in several ways depending on whether adjoining landmasses are seen as one or two, so the number depends on that choice. (e) The seven-continent count, because it is the one most widely adopted and used.
s: (a) Ravi joined nothing (seven separate continents)
(b) Salma joined the Americas and Europe with Asia
(c) Tenzin also joined Africa with Eurasia
(d) Same land, different grouping of adjoining landmasses
(e) Seven, as it is the most widely used

questions.q: Which is the largest island in the world, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Greenland

questions.q: The Indian Antarctica Programme began in 1981, and India set up its first scientific base station in Antarctica in 1983. How many years after the programme began was this base set up?
questions.a: 2 years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Australia is counted as an island because it is surrounded by water on all sides.
Reason (R): Continents are also surrounded by water, but because they are so large, they are not considered islands.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. India has set up three scientific base stations in Antarctica in all.
II. Antarctica is a continent with a very cold climate and a harsh environment.
III. The Indian Antarctica Programme began only after the Dakshin Gangotri base was set up.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: Explain the term 'island' as the chapter uses it, and give one example of an island group that belongs to India.
questions.a: An island is a smaller piece of land surrounded by water on all sides. Example: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (or the Lakshadweep Islands).
s: States that an island is a smaller piece of land surrounded by water on all sides
Names the Andaman and Nicobar Islands or the Lakshadweep Islands

questions.q: (a) In which water body does each of India's two major island groups lie? (b) A newspaper writes that the 2004 tsunami severely affected 'India's island group in the Arabian Sea'. Use (a) and the chapter's account of 2004 to correct it.
questions.a: (a) The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal; the Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea. (b) The chapter says the Andaman and Nicobar Islands were severely affected in 2004; by (a) that group is in the Bay of Bengal, so the newspaper should say 'India's island group in the Bay of Bengal', not the Arabian Sea.
s: (a) Andaman and Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal; Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea
(b) Corrects it to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal

questions.q: True or False? 'The Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea; it is the Andaman and Nicobar Islands that lie in the Bay of Bengal.
s: Gives the verdict False
Corrects it: Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea (Andaman and Nicobar is in the Bay of Bengal)

questions.q: A travel brochure says: 'Sail to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, part of India's 300 islands. Then fly to Greenland, the largest continent in the world, and end your trip in Antarctica, where India set up its first base station, Dakshin Gangotri, in 1993.' Find and correct the three errors using the chapter.
questions.a: 1. India has more than 1,300 islands, not 300. 2. Greenland is the largest island in the world, not a continent. 3. Dakshin Gangotri was set up in 1983, not 1993.
s: Corrects the number: India has more than 1,300 islands
Corrects Greenland: it is the world's largest island, not a continent
Corrects the year: Dakshin Gangotri was set up in 1983

questions.q:
In 2026 a Class 6 class in Pune writes to an Indian scientist at India's research settlement in Antarctica. She replies: 'I reached here after a long sea voyage. Outside, almost everything is ice and it is bitterly cold. We have a library and even a post office here, so your letter will carry a stamp from this faraway place! My team studies how the climate and environment have changed over time.' The class must choose one fact for its notice board.
(a) How many years before 2026 did the Indian Antarctica Programme begin?
(b) What was the name of India's first base station there, and in which year was it set up?
(c) The five Olympic rings stand for five continents. Why is Antarctica not one of them?
(d) The class can display only one of these: 'About 40 teams of Indian scientists have done research in Antarctica' or 'The settlement has a post office'. Which better shows India's work there, and why?
questions.a: (a) The programme began in 1981, so 2026 - 1981 = 45 years before. (b) Dakshin Gangotri, set up in 1983. (c) The rings represent the five inhabited continents (Africa, America, Asia, Australia and Europe); Antarctica, with its very cold climate and harsh environment, is not one of them; it is a place where teams of scientists carry out research. (d) Either is accepted with a reason; the stronger choice is the 40 teams, because it shows India's long and serious research on the evolution of climate and environment, while the post office only shows that scientists live there.
s: (b) Dakshin Gangotri, 1983
(c) The rings stand for inhabited continents; Antarctica, cold and harsh, is not one
(d) Chooses a fact and justifies it by what it shows about India's research

questions.q: Greenland and Antarctica are both large pieces of land with water on all sides. A student says, 'Since both are surrounded by water, either both are islands or both are continents.' Evaluate her claim: (a) What is each of them, according to the chapter? (b) What does the chapter use to tell an island from a continent? (c) Greenland is as big as India's 10 largest states put together. Does this make it a continent? (d) Give your verdict on her claim.
questions.a: (a) Greenland is an island (the largest in the world); Antarctica is a continent. (b) Size: continents are also surrounded by water, but they are so large that they are not considered islands; islands are smaller pieces of land surrounded by water. (c) No. Being as big as 10 Indian states makes Greenland the largest island, but the chapter still calls it an island, not a continent. (d) Her claim is wrong: being surrounded by water does not decide it, because both islands and continents have water around them; the difference is size, so one can be an island and the other a continent.
s: (a) Greenland is an island; Antarctica is a continent
(b) The difference is size, since continents too are surrounded by water
(c) No; it is still the largest island
(d) Verdict: the claim is wrong, water all around does not decide it

questions.q: More than half of the world's oxygen is produced by the oceans' flora. What name does this give the oceans, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The planet's lungs

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as a cause of the decline of marine life?
questions.a: Overfishing, that is, excessive fishing
o: Monsoon clouds forming over the ocean
Seawater flowing from one ocean into another

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with what the chapter links it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. 8 June  2. Tales of sea gods, sea monsters and treasures from the sea  3. Several million tonnes every year  4. Rain that the oceans send to the continents
Column B: a. World Oceans Day  b. the cultures of coastal people  c. plastic waste thrown into the oceans  d. the Earth's water cycle
A school poster says: 'The oceans' flora makes about one-third of the world's oxygen.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: It makes more than half of the world's oxygen, which is why the oceans are called the planet's lungs.
o: It makes more than half of the world's oxygen, which is why the oceans are called the planet's lungs.
It makes about three-fourths of the world's oxygen, the same as the share of the surface that is water.
It makes about one-fourth of the world's oxygen, the same as the share of the surface that is land.
It makes all of the world's oxygen, since plants on land make none.

questions.q: State two ways in which people have used the oceans and seas from early times, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: to migrate to other regions; to trade in all kinds of goods; to conduct military campaigns; as a source of food through fishing.
s: Gives one correct use (migration, trade, military campaigns or fishing for food)
Gives a second, different correct use

questions.q: (a) What do the words 'marine' and 'flora' mean? (b) Using both words, say in one sentence what produces more than half of the world's oxygen.
questions.a: (a) 'Marine' means related to or found in the oceans and seas; 'flora' means the plant life of a region. (b) The marine flora, the plant life of the oceans, produces more than half of the world's oxygen.
s: (a) Gives both meanings: marine (of the oceans and seas) and flora (plant life)
(b) States that marine flora (the oceans' plant life) produces more than half of the oxygen

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Of which natural cycle is the rain that oceans send to the continents a part? (b) What would the Earth become without oceans, according to the chapter? (c) Name one form of human activity that the chapter says is polluting the oceans.
questions.a: (a) The Earth's water cycle. (b) There would be no rainfall, and the Earth would be a desert. (c) Throwing plastic waste into the oceans (several million tonnes every year).
s: (a) The water cycle
(b) No rainfall; the Earth would be a desert
(c) Throwing plastic waste into the oceans

questions.q: A Class 6 group lists four 'gifts of the oceans': 1. more than half of the world's oxygen; 2. food through fishing; 3. drinking water for people; 4. complete safety for the people who live on the coasts. Check the list against the chapter: which gifts are supported, and what is wrong with the others?
questions.a: Gifts 1 and 2 are supported: the oceans' flora produces more than half of the world's oxygen, and people have used the oceans as a source of food through fishing. Gift 3 is wrong: seawater is salty and unfit for drinking by most land animals, including humans. Gift 4 is wrong: the oceans also give rise to cyclones and tsunamis that cause widespread damage to coastal areas.
s: Identifies gifts 1 and 2 as supported
Rejects gift 3: seawater is salty and unfit to drink
Rejects gift 4: cyclones and tsunamis damage coastal areas

questions.q:
A volunteer group cleans one beach in Puri every month and weighs the plastic it collects: January 120 kg, February 150 kg, March 180 kg. Local fishing families also tell the group that their catch has been falling year after year. Next month the group has volunteers for only one activity: another beach clean-up, or a talk with the fishing families about how much fish to catch.
(a) How much plastic did the group collect in the three months together?
(b) If the amount keeps rising by the same amount each month, how much will it collect in April?
(c) According to the chapter, what does plastic waste in the oceans do to marine life?
(d) Which activity should the group choose next month? Decide, using the data and both causes of decline that the chapter names.
questions.a: (a) 120 + 150 + 180 = 450 kg. (b) It rises by 30 kg a month, so 180 + 30 = 210 kg. (c) It chokes marine life and puts the marine environment under threat. (d) Either choice is accepted if both causes are weighed, for example: the clean-up, because the plastic found is rising every month; or the talk, because the falling catch points to overfishing, the other cause of decline that a clean-up cannot touch.
s: (b) 210 kg, from a rise of 30 kg a month
(c) Plastic chokes marine life
(d) Decides, weighing plastic pollution against overfishing with the data

questions.q: Write a five-line 'Ocean Report Card' for the Earth, using the chapter. For lines (a) to (d), give one fact and say whether it is good news or a worry: (a) oxygen; (b) rainfall; (c) plastic; (d) fishing. In line (e), give your overall judgement on what people should do, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Good news: the oceans' flora produces more than half of the world's oxygen, so they are called the planet's lungs. (b) Good news: the oceans send rain to the continents as part of the water cycle; without them the Earth would be a desert. (c) A worry: several million tonnes of plastic waste are thrown into the oceans every year, choking marine life. (d) Both: fishing has been a source of food since early times, but overfishing is causing a decline in marine life. (e) The oceans sustain life on Earth but are under threat from human activity, so protecting them is our collective responsibility.
s: (a) Oxygen: more than half from ocean flora, good news
(b) Rainfall from the oceans through the water cycle, good news
(c) Plastic waste chokes marine life, a worry
(d) Fishing gives food but overfishing reduces marine life
(e) Judges that the oceans need our collective protection, with a reason
